newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian dollar at a loss for direction.
newsitem.headline: Australian dollar at a loss for direction.

text.p: The Australian dollar drifted in a tight channel at the midsession as weeks of range-trading left the market desperate for fresh direction.

Dealers said the currency was sandwiched between good bids around US$0.7730, partly exporter and options related, and offers at US$0.7780 with some U.S. and German banks noteable sellers recently. A moment of excitement came when the yen surged in reaction to a huge jump in Japan's trade surplus, but quickly ran into heavy sales and retraced its steps.
Most expected the range to hold at least until the outcome of Tuesday's U.S. Federal Reserve policy meeting was know.
By 12.15 pm (0215 GMT) the local currency was hovering at US$0.7744/49 having hardly moved from its early US$0.7749/54 and was little changed on Friday's late US$0.7750/55 either.
On the crosses it dipped as low as 89.07 in the wake of the Japanese trade data but had bounced to 89.65/75 by midday, although that still left it a yen short of Friday's 90.50/60.
Japan's April surplus ballooned by 164 percent on the same month last year to reach 831 billion yen while the surplus with the U.S. rose an even stronger 174 percent.
The stronger trend was largely due to the past weakness of the yen and was expected to stretch for a few months yet.
That in turn was likely to strain Japan's trade relations with the U.S. as well as pointing to a sharp increase in the net demand for yen by offshore buyers of Japanese goods.
US$/yen took it hard at first, falling over 1/2 yen to 115.00 in a matter of minutes but by midday had rallied to 115.70/80 partly on Japanese demand.

One dealer who had just come back from a client visit to Tokyo said Japanese life offices remained doggedly bullish on US$/yen. "Many feel the Japanese banking system is just too fragile to bear a BOJ rate rise, so interest differentials will stay strongly in the dollar's favour," she said.

"They also reckon at least one major (Japanese) financial institution will fail before year-end and revive the dollar's safe haven status," she said. "Some even suspect the MOF has engineered the recent rise in the yen to provide a buffer for when the bad news breaks."
In trade weighted terms the local currency was off at 58.8 from 59.2 late Friday.

On the domestic front offshore investors could be forgiven for thinking the risk of another rate cut had been put to rest last week when Reserve Bank governor Ian Macfarlane said he saw no economic benefit in an easing.
He also underlined his concerns about wages noting growth in aggregate earnings had been a setback to the inflation outlook.

Analysts, however, noted average weekly earnings growth in most of 1996 had been led by big rises in the public sector. This was thought to be a function of wide-scale redundancies amongst lower paid public workers which boosted average wage growth to an annual 7.6 percent in Q4 last year.

In contrast private sector earnings -- which have for more relevance to inflationary pressures in the economy -- had been running at just 2.8 percent year-on-year in Q4 and another subdued result this time could leave space for a cut.

The rate was likely to rise in Q1 since a low 0.3 percent quarterly rise from Q1 1996 would fall out of the calculation. A repeat of the 0.8 percent gain seen in Q4, for instance, would take annual growth to around 3.3 percent.
"Private sector earnings will almost certainly push above 3.0 percent," said UBS Australia economist Stephen Roberts.

"But if the annual increase is above 3.5 percent the RBA will maintain a very wary weather watch on wages and be much less likely to consider further rate cuts if economic growth remains relatively soft over coming months," he said.
A survey of wage trends from HSBC did not bode well here.

The survey found wages growth in enterprise bargaining agreements had probably picked up in the March quarter to around 4.65 percent from the 4.4 percent reported by the Department of Industrial Relations (DIR) in the December quarter.

HSBC Markets economist Grant Fitzner said growth had been driven by a jump in private sector wage bargains and he expected the DIR measure of private sector wages would rise to around 4.9 percent from an annual 4.4 percent in Q4 1996.
The DIR is aiming to release its figures this week and perhaps as soon as Wednesday.
